desc:
Each row of rows is sorted in non-decreasing order (a row may be empty, and a value may repeat inside a row). Merge all rows into a single array that is sorted in strictly increasing order, so that every value that occurs anywhere in the input appears exactly once.

rows = [[1, 4, 4, 9], [2, 4, 8], [], [1, 9]]
answer = [1, 2, 4, 8, 9]

If every row is empty the answer is the empty array.
constraints: The total number of values is at most 5,000
Every row is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Putting everything in one array and sorting works. The point of this exercise is to use the fact that every row is already sorted.
The smallest value not yet used is always at the front of one of the rows. You only ever need to compare the current front of each row.
Keep a min-heap of (value, row, position) for the front of each non-empty row. Pop the smallest, append it unless it equals the last appended value, then push the next value of the same row.
editorial: This is the classic k-way merge. A min-heap holds at most one entry per row: the first value of that row which has not been consumed yet. Popping the heap yields values in globally sorted order; after each pop the next value of the same row is pushed.

Because the output is sorted, duplicates arrive next to each other, so removing them only needs a comparison with the last value written. Each of the N values is pushed and popped once, and the heap never holds more than k entries, so the time is O(N log k) with O(k) extra space besides the output.

Flattening and calling sorted(set(...)) is O(N log N) and fine in practice, but it ignores the sortedness of the input; the heap version is what interviewers expect, and it also works when the rows are streams that cannot be loaded at once.
